blocks.title: Fully qualified syntax
blocks.md:
Two traits may define methods with the same name, and a type may implement both, plus have its own inherent method of that name. By default `person.fly()` calls the **inherent** method. To call a trait's version, name the trait: `Pilot::fly(&person)`.

Associated **functions** without `self` are harder: `Animal::baby_name()` does not say which type's implementation you want. **Fully qualified syntax** names both: `<Dog as Animal>::baby_name()`. In general: `<Type as Trait>::function(receiver_if_method, next_arg, ...)`.

blocks.title: Supertraits
blocks.md: A trait can depend on another: `trait OutlinePrint: fmt::Display` means every `OutlinePrint` type must also be `Display`, so the default method may call `to_string()`. You met this in chapter 18. Forgetting the supertrait's impl gives a clear error:

blocks.title: The newtype pattern and the orphan rule
blocks.md:
The **orphan rule** (chapter 10) says you may implement a trait for a type only if the trait or the type is local to your crate. So you cannot implement `Display` for `Vec<String>`: both are from the standard library.

The workaround is a **newtype**: a tuple struct with one field, `struct Wrapper(Vec<String>);`. `Wrapper` is local, so you can implement anything on it. There is no run-time cost; the wrapper disappears at compile time. The downside is that `Wrapper` does not have `Vec`'s methods; implement `Deref` to get them all, or forward only the ones you want.

blocks.title: Money that cannot be mixed up
blocks.md: `Cents(i64)` is a newtype. Implement `Add` (cents + cents), `Mul<i64>` (cents * count), `Sum` so `iter().copied().sum::<Cents>()` works, and `Display` that prints `€12.34` (and `-€0.50` for negatives).
hints: `impl Sum for Cents { fn sum<I: Iterator<Item = Cents>>(iter: I) -> Cents { iter.fold(Cents(0), |a, b| a + b) } }`
`{:02}` pads the cents to two digits.

blocks.title: A 2D vector type
blocks.goal: Overload arithmetic, compound assignment, negation and indexing, use a default type parameter, and disambiguate same-named trait methods.
hints: Two impls of `Mul` with different `Rhs`: `impl Mul<f64> for Vec2` and `impl Mul<Vec2> for Vec2`.
`IndexMut` requires `Index`: `fn index_mut(&mut self, i: usize) -> &mut f64`.
Call the two methods as `Shape::name(v)` and `Label::name(v)`.
blocks.solution_explain: `Mul` is implemented twice with different `Rhs` type parameters, and each picks its own associated `Output`. A plain `v.name()` would be ambiguous because both traits are in scope; naming the trait settles it.

questions.q: Why is `Iterator::Item` an associated type rather than a generic parameter?
options: So each type implements Iterator once, and next() needs no annotations

questions.q: What does `Rhs = Self` in `trait Add<Rhs = Self>` mean?
options: Rhs defaults to Self when an impl does not specify it

points: Associated types: one implementation per type; generics: many.
Default type parameters (`Rhs = Self`) keep common impls short.
std::ops traits overload operators, including `+=`, unary `-` and indexing.
`<Type as Trait>::f()` disambiguates identically named functions.
Supertraits require other traits; newtypes get around the orphan rule at no cost.

terms.def: A type placeholder declared in a trait with type Name; and chosen by each implementation.
A generic parameter with a default, such as Rhs = Self.
Implementing std::ops traits so operators like + work on your types.
<Type as Trait>::function(...), naming both the type and the trait.
You may implement a trait for a type only if the trait or the type is defined in your crate.
A tuple struct with one field that wraps another type to give it a new identity.
